narrative:
The model predicts you have a 39% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three factors. By far the strongest influence is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of past failures is zero, so this history pulls the prediction strongly toward failing. Your number of school absences is the second most important factor; you had zero absences compared to an average of nearly four among students who passed. This actually helps your chances by pushing the prediction toward passing. The third key factor is your father’s education level, which is secondary. This also nudges the outcome slightly toward passing compared with students whose fathers have lower education.

In short, your past academic failure outweighs the positive effects of perfect attendance and your father’s education, leading the model to expect you may not pass without extra support.

To improve, focus first on preventing any further failures by seeking help early in difficult subjects. Keep your strong attendance record, and consider using the extra study time many passing students rely on. Taking the remedial courses seriously will give you the best chance to close the gap and succeed next year. (218 words)
